newsitem.title: USA: Republicans retain control of Congress - networks.
newsitem.headline: Republicans retain control of Congress - networks.

text.p: Republicans retained control of the Senate in Tuesday's congressional elections and television networks said it appeared they would also keep their majority in the House of Representatives.
The Republicans won open Senate seats previously held by Democrats in Alabama, Nebraska and President Bill Clinton's home state of Arkansas.

In early returns in the House most of the freshmen swept to victory in Republican takeover two years ago were fending off challenges. Democrats needed 19 seats to win control and had picked up five in early returns.
Democrats had been ready to celebrate gains of Republican Senate seats in New Hampshire and Maine, but the two parties remained locked in tight races there.

Currently Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate and 34 seats were at stake in the election. Democrats needed a net gain of three seats to win control, assuming Vice President Al Gore was there to break a tie vote.

In the House the party breakdown was 235-197, with one independent and two vacant seats. The outcome in the House, where all 435 seats were up for election, was likely to remain in doubt for some time although TV networks were projecting their would be no change in control.
The key to the control of the House appeared to lie largely with 70 freshmen seeking re-election -- and most of them appeared to be winning.
They had been swept into the House in the Republican "revolution" led by Speaker Newt Gingrich in 1994. Gingrich was re-elected in his Georgia district on Tuesday.

In the Arkansas Senate race, Republican Tim Hutchinson defeated Democrat Winston Bryant for the open seat held by retiring Sen. David Pryor to become the first Republican senator to be elected from that state since post-Civil War Reconstruction.

In Alabama Republican Jeff Sessions defeated Democrat Roger Bedford for the seat held by retiring Democrat Howell Heflin and in Nebraska Republican Chuck Angel beat Democratic Gov. Ben Nelson for the seat of retiring Democrat James Exon.
In New Hampshire, television networks had reported that Democrat Dick Swett had defeated Republican Sen Robert Smith. But the call was premature and the result was undecided.

Democrats won hard-fought races to retain seats in Massachusetts, New Jersey, Georgia and Illinois. Republicans kept two open seats in Kansas, vacated by presidential candidate Bob Dole and Sen. Nancy Kassebaum. They also held onto Senate seats in North and South Carolina, Tennessee, Oklahoma and Mississippi.

Voters re-elected two of the Senate's most prominent conservatives -- Jesse Helms of North Carolina and 93-year-old Strom Thurmond of South Carolina who aims to celebrate his 100th birthday as a senator in six years.

Thurmond, who will be 94 on Dec. 5, fended off a challenge by Democrat Elliott Close, to head into his eighth six-year term. Helms defeated the black former mayor of Charlotte, Harvey Gantt, in a replay of their contest six years ago.
Their race was the most expensive among the Senate contests, according to the watchdog group Common Cause. Helms spent more than $19 million and Gantt more than $6 million.

In New Jersey Democratic Representative Robert Torricelli defeated conservative Republican Dick Zimmer for the Senate seat vacated by Democrat Bill Bradley. The race had been marked by furious mudslinging ads from both sides.

In Massachusetts Democratic Sen. John Kerry won a third term in a high-profile race with popular Gov. William Weld. In Illinois Representative Richard Durbin defeated Republican Al Salvi, winning the open seat vacated by Democrat Paul Simon.
In Georgia triple amputee Max Cleland, former head of the Veterans Administration, held the Senate seat vacated by fellow Democrat Sam Nunn, defeating Republican Guy Millner.
